Dear Yamini,
You asked me to tell you how it went. I reported a senior who kept sending me messages after I asked him to stop. On Monday the head of department called me in and said, “A complaint like this will damage the college’s name, and the accreditation visit is next month. Are you sure?”
I went home feeling guilty and afraid. I typed a withdrawal note twice and deleted it.
This afternoon I took the message to Dr. Rao, the ombuds officer. She said the complaint was mine to keep and that the college’s name was not mine to guard. She opened the file that same day and introduced me to the counsellor.
I haven’t withdrawn.
Vinita

passage: Placement week, and Saurabh was called to the HOD's cabin between two interviews. Dr Hemant Joshi didn't offer him a seat. "You emailed the university about the leaked mid-sem paper?" "Sir, I saw it shared in the hostel group the night before." "And did you think of the college's name? Of the companies sitting downstairs right now? Of your batchmates' jobs?" Two other professors in the room said nothing, eyes on their files. Dr Joshi slid a sheet across. "A simple withdrawal. You were mistaken. Everyone moves on." Saurabh's mouth went dry. He felt, absurdly, like the one who had cheated. His next interview was in ten minutes. He picked up the pen. Then he put it down. "Sir, can I think about it tonight?" In the corridor he called his aunt, a lecturer in Pune. "Don't sign anything under pressure," she said. "Tonight we'll read the university's grievance rules together."

qa.q: What had Saurabh emailed the university about?
qa.a: About the leaked mid-sem paper.

qa.a: He didn't sign under pressure and asked for time, then called his aunt; reading the grievance rules with her is a safe next step.

qa.a: They may have felt uneasy about the pressure but afraid to cross the HOD, so they kept their eyes on their files.

grounding: Shows a student who reported cheating being told it will harm the college's name, feeling guilt and fear, and nearly withdrawing.
